title: Two HD 93683 fits require a nonzero outer velocity amplitude during 1991-2026 under a quadrupole model
abstract: An eccentric inner binary can change sky inclination with a face-on outer orbit at one instant. We derive a finite-interval velocity test from conservation of total orbital angular momentum. A measured range Z of the inner line-of-sight angular momentum forces the outer orbit to tilt: max sin(i2) is at least sqrt(d(2-d)) for d=Z/L2 up to one, and is one for d from one to two. We allow all photometric inclination branches and bounded changes in inner eccentricity. Combining this result with a published quadrupole torque bound removes the outer period and eccentricity for each stated companion mass. The circular outer orbit gives the weakest bound. For the first HD 93683 point fit, inner masses of 18 and 15 solar masses, a global inner eccentricity cap of 0.267655, and third-star masses of 8, 15 and 25 solar masses, the outer binary-centre velocity semi-amplitude must reach 4.25, 4.80 and 5.21 km/s during the fitted interval. We give a second fit, eccentricity sensitivity tests, proofs and numerical checks. These are conditional necessary bounds, not velocity detections or guarantees at observing visits. The global eccentricity cap, secular dynamics and adopted photometric fits limit the result.

display.caption: Finite-interval lower velocity bounds for three stated third-star masses. The circular outer orbit gives the weakest bound after the torque test removes outer period and eccentricity. The right panel varies the assumed maximum inner eccentricity.
